## The short version {.section-title}

::: {.prose}
I am a Ph.D. student in the Evolution and Society area of the Department of
Psychology at the University of New Mexico. My research focuses on the
evolutionary and developmental foundations of human social relationships and
sexual behavior. Much of my work examines cross-sex friendships, relationship
dynamics, and the developmental pathways that shape variation in sexual
behavior.

I am broadly interested in integrating multiple methodological approaches—including
genetically informed designs, longitudinal and intensive longitudinal data, and
hormonal measures—to better understand how biological and environmental
processes jointly influence human social and mating behavior.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.band .band-cream}
::: {.wrap}
[Research]{.eyebrow}

## What I work on {.section-title}

::: {.section-intro}
Three threads run through my work. Each one asks how biological and
environmental processes jointly shape human social and mating behavior.
:::

::: {.card-grid}

::: {.c-card}
[01]{.c-card-num}

### Cross-sex friendship and courtship

How mating motivations shape friendships between men and women, and how
courtship behavior is signalled and perceived within them.

::: {.tags}
[Mating psychology]{.tag}
[Relationships]{.tag}
:::
:::

::: {.c-card}
[02]{.c-card-num}

### Hormones and the ovulatory cycle

How women's sexual psychology and emotional states shift across the cycle,
and what estradiol and progesterone have to do with it.

::: {.tags}
[Intensive longitudinal]{.tag}
[Endocrinology]{.tag}
:::
:::

::: {.c-card}
[03]{.c-card-num}

### Sexual development and behavior genetics

Using genetically informed designs to separate environmental effects from
genetic confounding in how families shape sexual development.

::: {.tags}
[Adoption designs]{.tag}
[Sibling comparison]{.tag}
:::
:::

:::
:::
:::
